Engineering Case Study · Vue 3 + React · MIT License

Admin Builder — one framework, two frontends, one contract

A reusable admin-panel framework, extracted from years of rebuilding the same list-filter-modal pattern for different clients — then proven portable by rebuilding the entire thing again in a second frontend framework, on purpose.

Oleksandr Nosov
Full-stack engineer
github.com/alex-no/admin
admin.4n.com.ua
01 · Origin
Why I built this

The same panel, rebuilt one too many times

During years of commercial development I built and maintained a lot of admin panels. The business logic was never the same — service directories, e-commerce backoffices, internal tools — but the admin interface underneath kept rhyming: a data table with filters and pagination, a details form, localization, auth, roles, a settings screen.

I watched that pattern get hand-rebuilt slightly differently on nearly every project — most visibly on AllSTO, a production project of mine, where admin list pages piled up over time and the same filter / sort / CSV-export / inline-edit features ended up wired a little differently on each one.

So instead of writing it again, I pulled it out into its own project. Admin Builder is the result — a reusable constructor for admin panels that works against any REST API.

Live demo · admin.4n.com.ua
02 · Goals
What I optimized for

Goals, going in

  • Reusable architecture — mechanics live in the framework, not copy-pasted onto every page.
  • A framework-independent contract — the frontend depends on an API shape, not on Yii3, PHP, or any particular backend.
  • Two working frontends, not a slideware claim — Vue and React, same features, same behavior.
  • Drop-in integration — copy the mechanics into an existing project, describe the entity in JSON, done.
  • Fast delivery of internal business tools — the kind of app that shouldn't take three weeks to bootstrap.
  • Something I can actually walk through in an interview — real trade-offs, not a features list.
03 · Architecture
Architecture

Where the boundary actually is

Browserend user
→
FrontendVue 3 or React — chosen once, per project
→
shared/coreframework-agnostic TypeScript
→
REST contractlist · patch · bulk · pagination shape
→
Backendany language — Yii3 + PHP in the demo
→
Databaseowned by the backend

The frontend holds no business logic and only ever speaks through the REST contract — that part is the headline architecture. The part that actually makes it work is shared/core: the Vue composables and the React hooks are thin wrappers around the same plain-TypeScript modules (modal-window state, URL state, permissions). Zero npm dependencies inside shared/core — it genuinely doesn't know which framework is holding it.

04 · Stack
Technology stack

Modern, and nothing extra

◆Frontend · Vue

Vue 3.5 (Composition API), Vite, Vue Router 5, vue-i18n, Bootstrap 5. The reference implementation — where behavior is ambiguous, Vue wins.

◆Frontend · React

React 18.3 + TypeScript 5.7, Vite, React Router 7, react-i18next, the same Bootstrap 5. A full port — same pages, same contract, checked by tsc in the build.

◆shared/core

Plain TypeScript, no runtime dependencies. Imported by both frontends so the two implementations can't quietly diverge on logic.

◆Backend (demo)

Yii3 on PSR (DI / router / middleware), raw PDO over SQLite — no ORM — seeded from CSV. Deliberately disposable, see slide 09.

◆API & docs

REST + Swagger via zircote/swagger-php, one response contract shared by both frontends.

◆DevOps

Docker Compose — separate dev containers per frontend, one Apache+PHP container in production serving both builds under two vhosts.

No Redux
No Pinia
State lives in the URL and local hooks — see slide 07
05 · Decision 1
Decision 1 · list-framework

Config, not copy-paste

Problem

A new entity meant copying an existing list page and hand-editing table markup, filters and pagination — every copy drifted a little further from the original. In one production project this happened on dozens of admin pages.

Decision

Columns, filters and endpoints for a list page are three JSON files, read by one shared list component. Sorting, bulk edit, column visibility and live-refresh aren't configured — they come built into the component itself.

Trade-off

Genuinely one-off screens don't get to be JSON — and the project says so explicitly: two legacy analytics pages are flagged in the README as "not a pattern to copy," on purpose, instead of being forced onto a framework they don't fit.

Data registry — list + filter + sort
06 · Decision 2
Decision 2 · BaseModal

One modal component, three shapes

Detail views needed to work as a quick floating peek, a docked side panel that doesn't cover the list underneath, and a full-height bottom panel for busy screens. Instead of three components — or three ad-hoc copies of the same modal markup — there is exactly one, switched between the three modes, with drag-resize and the chosen mode remembered per user. No page owns its own modal markup; content comes in through slots. The cost is a slot-based API instead of quick one-off markup — worth it, since there are zero competing modal implementations left to keep in sync.

Floating
Docked right
Docked bottom
07 · Decision 3
Decision 3 · state

The URL is the state manager

Problem

Shareable state

Filters, multi-column sort, page size and which record's detail card is open all need to survive a reload and be shareable as a plain link — the textbook case for a global store.

Decision

No store was added

A single composable/hook reads and writes exactly that slice of state to the URL query string. Everything else stays local component state.

Trade-off

A bet on the domain

This holds because an admin CRUD table doesn't need state shared across unrelated pages. A more stateful app would need to revisit it — it's a fit, not a rule.

08 · Reality check
Proving portability

I didn't just claim it was portable — I rebuilt it

frontend-react/ is a full second implementation — same pages, same behavior, same backend — built specifically to test whether the architecture holds outside Vue, not just inside it. Directory structure and contracts landed almost file-for-file identical. Where they didn't, the README says so instead of hiding it:

WhereVueReactWhy it differs
Page ↔ modalwindow.dispatchEventplain props / stateNo built-in global event bus in React — props are the idiomatic equivalent
i18n scopeuseI18n() defaults to a local instance per componentuseTranslation() is always globalA real Vue gotcha: without useScope:'global' everywhere, a language switch silently misses components
Route gatingrouter checks only "is there a token"dedicated RequirePermission.tsxAdded on the React side after the port surfaced the gap
Docked-modal marginevery page wraps itself in ListPageWrapper.vueone hook, wired once in the root layoutReact applies it globally; double-wrapping a page would double the margin

None of these are bugs — they're the seams where "the same architecture" meets two frameworks' idioms, written down on purpose so the next port doesn't have to rediscover them.

09 · Decision 4
Decision 4 · the backend is disposable

This backend throws its data away on purpose

The demo backend (Yii3 + SQLite, seeded from CSV) resets every time its container restarts. That's not a bug — it's the point.

The deliverable of this project is the frontend and the REST contract it expects (list / pagination / patch / bulk shape) — not a production backend. Swap it for anything that speaks that contract — Node, Rails, a different PHP stack — and the frontend doesn't change.

Building a "real" backend here would have been effort spent proving the wrong thing.

Swagger — the contract, not the implementation
10 · AI-assisted
Force multiplier

Designed to be extended by an agent, not just by me

A stated goal from the start was using AI assistants (Claude Code) to extend the project, not only to build it. That only works if the codebase is legible to an agent — so the mechanics are deliberately small, documented, uniform files: JSON configs and typed registries, instead of clever logic spread across many places.

On top of that I wrote six Claude Code skills, committed to the repo itself — admin-integrate, admin-data-page, admin-dashboard-page, admin-audit-log, admin-optimistic-locking, list-framework-type — that encode the project's own conventions, so an agent adding a new entity follows the same pattern a human would.

Scoping decision

Two roadmap features — an audit log and optimistic locking — are deliberately not built into the demo. They ship as ready-to-run skills with a concrete plan (schema, code sample, where to surface it in the UI) instead, since nothing in this project actually needs them yet.

11 · Evolution
Evolution

From a symptom to a standing process

01

Symptom

The same list + filter + modal code hand-rebuilt, slightly differently, across dozens of pages in a production admin panel.

02

Extraction

Pulled the reusable mechanics into their own open-source, backend-agnostic project, released under MIT.

03

Feedback loop

Admin Builder is now the reference: new admin features are designed and tested here first, in both frontends, then ported into the production app's Vue admin.

Not a one-off portfolio artifact — an ongoing process that still runs today.

12 · Takeaways
What this is evidence of

What this project demonstrates

  • Extracting architecture from real, repeated pain — not from a tutorial (slides 01, 05).
  • Paying a real cost to test a claim instead of just asserting it — a full second frontend (slide 08).
  • Writing down where an abstraction leaks instead of hiding it (slide 08).
  • Scoping a personal project like a production one — shipping a design instead of unrequested code (slide 10).
  • Backend-agnostic API contract design (slide 09).
  • Treating AI-friendliness as an actual architectural requirement, not a buzzword (slide 10).
  • Technical writing — the README this deck is built from documents integration steps, contracts and known divergences in enough detail for another engineer, or an agent, to act on.
13 · Roadmap
Future development

What's next

  • More frontend frameworks — a further portability test, the same way React was.
  • A plugin architecture for cell/filter types, beyond the current runtime registry.
  • Audit log and optimistic locking — currently skills with a plan, applied for real.
  • A visual page-config designer — generate the three JSON files from a UI instead of by hand.
  • More reusable components, pulled out of client work as they come up.
